# Structured Append for Standard QR

## Purpose

Phase 5 of [featherqr-2.0.0-plan.md](featherqr-2.0.0-plan.md). Until Phase 5a the Standard QR decoder rejected a Structured Append symbol as `UnsupportedContent` the moment it saw the mode indicator; the generator still has no way to produce one. A caller whose data does not fit in one symbol of the size they can print had no path through the library in either direction, and still has none for producing a set. This plan fixes WHAT ships, in WHICH order, and WHY each rule is what it is. HOW each piece is verified follows the mandatory test-first workflow. When it completes, its durable content graduates into [standardqr-decoder.md](../specs/standardqr-decoder.md), [standardqr-encoder.md](../specs/standardqr-encoder.md) and the shared contract in [qrcode-symbologies.md](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md), the 2.0.0 plan's Phase 5 row gets its Progress log entry, and this file is deleted.

## Scope

| In | Out |
|---|---|
| Decode: read the header, report it on `QRCodeDecodeInfo`, return the symbol's own text | Micro QR and rMQR: neither symbology defines Structured Append, neither has a mode indicator for it, so no such stream can exist for them and their `*DecodeInfo` types gain nothing |
| Encode: one entry point that splits text across the fewest symbols the version cap allows, balanced so every symbol has the same version | A combine helper. Reassembly policy (missing symbols, duplicates, a parity mismatch) is the caller's; a helper that decides it cannot be removed later, and the four rules below are what a caller needs |
| Committed fixtures and oracle cross-checks in both directions | An explicit symbol-count overload ("always four symbols"). Additive in a minor if a request arrives; the version cap covers the case that motivates the feature |
| Spec and migration-guide updates in the same changes; the README feature line lands with 5d | A sizing API for "how many symbols would this take". Same reason; `TryGetRequiredBufferSize` stays single-symbol |
| | Playground and BlazorWasm sample. Untouched, as Phase 4 left them |

## The wire format and what it fixes

ISO/IEC 18004 places a 20-bit header in the bit stream: mode indicator `0011`, a 4-bit symbol position (0-based), a 4-bit total count minus one (so 1 to 16 symbols), and an 8-bit parity byte. Three consequences shape everything below.

**Every symbol decodes on its own.** The header is followed by ordinary mode segments, and each symbol carries its own segment plan, its own ECI header and its own terminator. So a split must fall on a character boundary, never inside a surrogate pair, or both halves decode to garbage; and the per-symbol capacity is the data capacity of the version minus the 20-bit header minus the ECI header the symbol repeats, so a set of N symbols holds less than N times one symbol.

**The parity byte identifies the set, not the content.** It is the XOR of the bytes of the whole input taken once, before splitting, in the one charset the set is written in, and every symbol carries the same value. A reader uses it to tell that symbols from two different sets have been mixed; it cannot verify the reassembled content with it, because it does not know the charset the encoder chose. That is why the charset is decided once for the whole text and repeated as an ECI header in every symbol: it is the only way "the bytes of the whole input" names one byte sequence.

**The header is a prefix, and a reader should not care where it is.** The encoder writes it first, before any ECI or data segment, so a decoder that stops at the first data segment can still find it. The decoder accepts it anywhere in the stream, because rejecting a symbol whose header sits after its ECI would refuse a symbol every other reader accepts, and the rejection buys nothing.

## Design

### Decode

`QRStructuredAppend` is a library-built `readonly record struct` in the core, non-positional with an internal constructor and get-only properties, the Phase 3 shape, and Standard QR-only by the naming rule (short `QR` prefix; it is not "a code").

| Member | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `int Index` | Position in the set, 0-based, as on the wire. `Index < Count` holds whenever the value is not empty; the empty value has both at 0 |
| `int Count` | Symbols in the set, 1 to 16 |
| `byte Parity` | The parity byte as read |
| `bool IsEmpty` | True when the symbol carried no header. `default` is empty, because a real header has `Count >= 1` |

`QRCodeDecodeInfo` gains `QRStructuredAppend StructuredAppend`, set by an internal constructor overload and carried by `WithCorners`, so the member order stays `Status, Version, EccLevel, MaskPattern, ErrorsCorrected, Corners, StructuredAppend`. Every entry point that returns a `QRCodeDecodeInfo` (five in the core, one in the rendering package) populates it; the matrix decoders read it from the bit stream, which is the one place the header exists.

Rules the bit-stream decoder enforces:

- The 20 bits are read and the segment loop continues. The text returned is this symbol's own.
- `Index >= Count` is `InvalidBitstream`. The two nibbles cannot encode a position outside the set; a symbol that does is malformed in the same class as a character count that overruns the stream, and the library refuses that class everywhere.
- A second header in one stream is `InvalidBitstream`.
- Fewer than 16 bits after the mode indicator is `InvalidBitstream`, as any truncated segment is.
- A header claiming a set of one is accepted and reported as `Index 0, Count 1`. Nothing in the standard forbids it, and the encoder below never writes it.

Reassembly rules for the caller, documented on the type and in the migration guide, and the whole of what a combine helper would have encoded:

1. All symbols report the same `Count` and the same `Parity`.
2. The indices `0 .. Count-1` are each present exactly once.
3. Text is concatenated in `Index` order.
4. `Parity` is a set identity. It is not a checksum of the concatenation, and a caller should not try to recompute it.

### Encode

```csharp
public static QRCodeData[] CreateStructuredAppend(ReadOnlySpan<char> text, QREccLevel eccLevel, in QRCodeGeneratorOptions options = default)
```

One method on `QRCodeGenerator`, beside `Create`. It takes the same options record, and the split is driven by `options.Version`, which already exists: "fewest symbols" is meaningless without a cap (version 40 holds 2,953 bytes, so the uncapped answer is always one symbol), and the cap is what a caller actually has, in the form "the largest symbol my label or my camera distance allows". `QRVersionRange.AtMost(n)` is that cap. No new parameter is added.

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| The text fits in one symbol within `options.Version` | One element, byte-identical to `Create(text, eccLevel, options)`. No header: a set of one costs 20 bits and tells a reader nothing |
| It needs 2 to 16 symbols | That many, all at one version, balanced, each carrying the header |
| It needs more than 16 at `Version.Max` | `ArgumentException` on `options`, as `Create` throws when the text does not fit |

**Balanced, not greedy.** Filling each symbol to capacity and letting the last one take the remainder gives a set of three version-10 symbols and one version-2 symbol; on the same label that reads as a defect. The split minimises the fill of the fullest symbol, so all symbols come out at one version, in three steps that each reuse the segment planner rather than adding a second capacity model:

1. Count the fewest symbols at `Version.Max`. Each symbol's payload capacity is the data capacity at that version and ECC level, less 20 bits, less the ECI header when the set carries one. Chunks are taken greedily at character boundaries, the boundary found by binary search on "does this prefix plan into the capacity", which is monotone in the prefix length. One symbol collapses to `Create`; more than sixteen throws.
2. Take the smallest version in `[Version.Min, Version.Max]` whose capacity still fits that count. Every symbol uses it.
3. Binary-search the smallest per-symbol capacity, at that version, that still fits the count, and split at that capacity. That is the balanced split.

Every chunk is planned by the existing segmenter at the actual version, so the count-indicator band is exact rather than approximated. Two symbols is the smallest set, so there is no version-1 edge case: a chunk that does not fit at all under the cap is the throw in step 1.

**Rules the encoder holds, and why:**

| Rule | Reason |
|---|---|
| The charset is decided once, from the whole text, by the existing analysis; every chunk is encoded with that charset forced, and the ECI header is written in every symbol | "The bytes of the whole input" must name one byte sequence. A pure-ASCII chunk of a UTF-8 set still carries the UTF-8 ECI |
| Parity is the XOR of that one byte sequence, computed from the whole text before splitting | Any per-chunk computation can diverge from it when a chunk would have chosen a different charset on its own |
| Header order is Structured Append, then ECI, then the segments | The encoder writes the ECI header first today; the Structured Append header goes in front of it |
| `Utf8Bom` is written in symbol 0 only and counted in the parity | It is a prefix of the data, as in the single-symbol path; repeating it would insert a BOM mid-text on reassembly |
| `BoostEccLevel` boosts the whole set to the level every symbol can take, or not at all | Boosting per symbol produces a set with mixed ECC levels, and a set that should look identical has no reason to differ there |
| `MaskPattern` applies to every symbol; `Segmentation` and `QuietZoneSize` apply per symbol | Same option, same meaning |
| Splits never fall inside a surrogate pair | The split operates on `char`s, so this is the only boundary hazard; UTF-8 byte boundaries follow from it |

## Decisions

| # | Decision | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Index base in the public type | 0-based, as on the wire. `Index < Count` holds directly; a 1-based `Index <= Count` is where off-by-one errors come from |
| S2 | Header position on decode | Accepted anywhere in the stream. Written first on encode |
| S3 | A set of one | Never written; accepted on read |
| S4 | `Index >= Count` on decode | `InvalidBitstream` |
| S5 | ECC boost across a set | Uniform |
| S6 | Symbol count driven by | `options.Version` (existing), not a new parameter. An explicit-count overload is additive later |
| S7 | Combine helper | Not shipped; rules documented |
| S8 | Interaction with Phase 6 (Kanji encode) | Parity is over the bytes the set is written in, so when Kanji mode lands the byte representation of Japanese text changes and so does its parity. Within one set the value stays consistent, so nothing breaks across readers, but any fixture that pins a parity byte for Japanese input moves. The decode corpus already holds Japanese text both ways, as UTF-8 with an ECI and as Kanji mode, because those are third-party symbols and the decoder must report whatever is on the wire; what Phase 6 moves is the parity this library's own encoder writes for Japanese input, so 5b pins its encoder-side parity on ASCII, Latin-1 and non-Japanese UTF-8 text only and Phase 6 adds the Japanese cases |

## Phases

Each phase follows the test-first workflow, regenerates `src/FeatherQR/PublicAPI.approved.txt`, updates `docs/migration.md` and the affected specs in the same change, and appends a Progress log entry with Done / Lessons / benchmark delta. No phase moves a hot path; each states so.

| # | Priority | Phase | Contents | Exit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5a | **P0** | Decode | `QRStructuredAppend`; `QRCodeDecodeInfo.StructuredAppend`; the bit-stream decoder reads the header and enforces the four rules; all decode overloads populate it; `TypeShapeTest` additions; the decoder spec's scope row flips; migration guide gains an additive section | A committed third-party four-symbol set (provenance recorded beside the files) decodes to four texts with `Index` 0 to 3, `Count` 4 and one shared `Parity`; hand-assembled bit streams cover the header anywhere, `Index >= Count`, a duplicate header, truncation, and a set of one; Micro QR and rMQR untouched (no mode indicator exists for it there) |
| 5b | **P1** | Encode | Header writer and parity; the three-step balanced split on the existing planner; `CreateStructuredAppend`; the option rules table above; the encoder spec's scope row flips | Round trip through 5a: for texts at every length up to sixteen symbols' worth, every symbol decodes, concatenation in index order equals the input, all symbols share one version and one parity, and the fullest symbol is no fuller than the balanced bound; one-symbol result byte-identical to `Create`; more than sixteen throws; each option rule has a test that fails when the rule is dropped |
| 5c | **P1** | Interop | Sets produced by 5b read by the pinned reader oracles in `tools/QRInteropFixtures` and by the pinned encoder oracles' own decoders where they have one; sets produced by the pinned encoder oracles read by 5a; committed fixtures; spot-check list for the Phase 8 release checklist | Every reader agrees with 5a on `Index`, `Count` and `Parity` for every generated set; the parity byte matches what the encoder oracles compute for the same input, byte for byte |
| 5d | P2 | Fold | Progress log entry on the 2.0.0 plan's Phase 5 row; README feature line; this plan folded into the three specs and deleted | The specs carry the rules and the decisions; nothing here is only here |

5a ships first because it is the half that can be verified against symbols this library did not make, and it is what 5b's round trip is measured through. 5b and 5c are one PR each. 5d is small and closes the plan.

## Verification notes

- Bit-stream tests drive `QRBinaryDecoder.DecodeBitStream` directly (internals are visible to the test project), so the header rules are pinned without any image or encoder in the loop.
- The balanced bound is a stated inequality, not "looks even": with `n` symbols and payload `P` bits, the fullest symbol holds at most the smallest capacity `c` for which `n` chunks suffice, and the test asserts exactly that.
- Mutation checks on 5b: drop the ECI repeat in symbols after the first, compute parity per chunk instead of once, split inside a surrogate pair, boost per symbol. Each must fail a test.
- Parity fixtures pin the byte for ASCII, Latin-1 and non-Japanese UTF-8 inputs (S8), and the 5c cross-check compares it with the encoder oracles on the same inputs, which is what proves the definition rather than the implementation.

## Progress log

Entries are appended per phase: what was done, what was learned, and an explicit statement that no hot path moved.

### Phase 5a, decode (2026-09-15)

**Done.** `QRStructuredAppend` (`Index` 0-based, `Count`, `Parity`, `IsEmpty`; a library-built `readonly record struct`, the Phase 3 shape) and `QRCodeDecodeInfo.StructuredAppend`, carried through `WithCorners` so every entry point that returns a `QRCodeDecodeInfo` (five in the core, one in the rendering package) reports it without the image decoders knowing. The bit-stream decoder reads the 20-bit header wherever it sits and refuses a position past the count, a second header and a truncated one as `InvalidBitstream`; the header is attached on `Success` only, like `Corners`. Micro QR and rMQR are untouched. Core listing 35 to 36 exported types, one member added, nothing else changed. The corpus came first: 95 symbols in 14 sets from two pinned in-process encoder lineages (a balancing one and an explicit-parts one) plus 4 third-party captures. Every generated symbol passed through the pinned reader gate, which supplies per-symbol text and the header values and checks the parity against the bytes the set carries; the captures are reader-sourced end to end, checked for one count, one parity and every index across the set and for their concatenation against the expected text. `StructuredAppendFixtureTest` (matrix and image path per symbol, the flipped-module control, the too-small-destination pin of the success-only rule, the four reassembly rules per set, the corpus shapes), `StructuredAppendDecodeTest` (thirteen hand-assembled streams: header first, after a segment, after an ECI, a set of one, the last of sixteen, no header, position past the count, a second header, a truncated header, and the 16-bit guard at 15, 16, 17 and 18 remaining bits, the last two being a header followed by the implicit terminator), `TypeShapeTest` extended, and `UnsupportedModes` loses mode 3. The decoder spec's scope row, the shared spec's two sentences and the migration guide follow. Full suite green on both target frameworks (9,907 tests on net10.0 after the review round below).

**The parity gate has to XOR the bytes the symbols carry, not the bytes a charset guess would produce.** The first gate assumed ISO-8859-1 when the text fitted it and UTF-8 otherwise, and it was wrong twice in one run: the explicit-parts lineage writes Latin-1 text as UTF-8 with an ECI, and Japanese text in Kanji mode with no ECI, both legitimate and both a different parity from the balancing lineage's for the same text (139 against 8; 6 against 176). The reader exposes the raw segment bytes, so the definition itself is checkable, and the corpus now holds those four symbols as its most valuable cases: a decoder has to report what is on the wire.

**A corpus that cannot fail is not a gate.** An even repetition of any text XORs to 0 in every charset, and an even number of accented characters in one 0xC0 block makes the ISO-8859-1 and UTF-8 parities coincide, so three of the seven first-draft sets would have passed a gate computing the parity over the wrong bytes. Every repetition count is odd now and the Latin-1 sentence carries seven accented characters per repetition.

**The gate caught an oracle.** The pinned balancing encoder at 3.1.0 wrote parity 0 on every set, the defect its 3.2.0 fixed; the pin is 3.2.1 now, and the fixture spec's oracle matrix says not to go below it.

**The corpus found a defect in a different component.** One symbol of ninety-nine, `sixteen-symbols-max-v2-l-2of16` of the explicit-parts lineage, reads through the matrix path and not from its clean 8 px render: the finder locator picks a false candidate three modules inside the real top-right finder, at 5 px/module and up. Not this phase's problem and not touched here; recorded as F10 in the 2.0.0 plan with the measurements, and the fixture test lists it as a known image-path defect behind a guard that fails when the locator is fixed.

**Benchmark delta.** Not measured: the decode path gains one `switch` case that runs only when the mode indicator is `0011`, and no hot path moved.

### Adversarial review of Phase 5a (2026-09-15)

**Done.** Three parallel reviewers over the change, three independent verifiers per claim, two rounds. Round one kept 19 of 20 claims; round two kept 9 of 10. No defect in the decoder's behaviour was found; what was found is that two of its rules were unpinned and that the documents around it had drifted.

**Two rules were enforced by one line each and no test noticed.** The "header on Success only" ternary in the matrix decoder could be deleted and 9,713 tests stayed green, because every stream test went straight to the bit-stream decoder and every fixture decoded; the 16-bit guard could become `< 15`, which lets the bit reader throw on a 15-bit remainder, and the seeded fuzz test never reaches that remainder (its two thousand streams happen to enter the case only with a multiple of four bits left; a numeric or alphanumeric segment ahead of the header leaves any remainder, as the new tests show). Both are pinned now: every matrix fixture is decoded into a one-character destination and must come back without the header (95 cases; the mutant fails all of them), and four streams sit exactly at 15, 16, 17 and 18 remaining bits, the last two a header followed by the implicit terminator (the `< 15` mutant fails the 15-bit one, `< 17` fails the 16-bit one).

**A corpus floor that counts symbols cannot notice a lost lineage.** `> 40` survives dropping either encoder lineage, the 2-set, the 16-set, the Kanji set or either charset-divergent pair. The corpus test now names each of those shapes, the way `KanjiFixtureTest` names its minimum counts. The class also gained the flipped-module negative control the fixture spec promised for every fixture class, and its data sources parse each manifest once instead of about two thousand times.

**The documents said three things the code did not.** Three XML comments, two of them on shipped public types, still called Structured Append unsupported, the six `info` parameter docs did not mention the member, and the committed Playground API page predates the change entirely; the plan named a `WithStructuredAppend` that never existed, counted "seven entry points" where six return a result, denied the corpus its two Japanese sets, and promised an `UnsupportedContent` from Micro QR and rMQR that neither can produce (neither has a mode indicator for it, so no such stream exists; the rMQR spec carried the same claim for FNC1). The migration sample used a C# 14-only spelling beside advice against it, then, after the first fix, an extension method that netstandard2.0 does not have; it now uses `ContainsKey` and leaves the message null until a whole set was seen. The fixture spec described the explicit-parts lineage's parity as "per part" when every symbol of a set carries one value, the XOR of the whole text in the charset that lineage writes it in.

**Tooling.** The importer refuses an incomplete capture set, a repeated index, a set whose symbols disagree on parity, and a version the reader could not name; the gate refuses an ECI header over ASCII-only bytes rather than guess which ECI it was.

**Lessons.** A rule that lives in one conditional needs a test that fails when the conditional is removed, and "every test passes" says nothing about that until someone removes it. A fuzz test with a fixed seed pins only the branches its seed happens to reach; the boundary cases have to be written by hand. Counting fixtures is not the same as naming them. And the generated API page has to be regenerated in the same change as the API, which the plan already recorded once and this change repeated.

**Benchmark delta.** Not measured: no production logic changed in the review; XML comments, tests and the fixture tooling only.

### Phase 5b, encode (2026-09-15)

**Done.** `QRCodeGenerator.CreateStructuredAppend(text, ecc, options)` returning `QRCodeData[]`, the one method the design table promised, and nothing else on the surface (listing +1 member). The split lives in `StructuredAppendPlanner`: a chunk's cost is its single-mode stream or, under `Optimal`, the cheaper of that and the minimal mixed plan, plus the 20-bit header and the ECI header the set repeats; cost is monotone in the chunk's length, so the longest chunk that fits a budget is a binary search and a greedy walk at a budget gives the count. The three searches of the design (fewest at the largest version, smallest version for that count, smallest budget at that version) are three loops over that walk. The header enters the stream through a `StructuredAppend` member on the encoder's configuration record, written first by `QRBinaryEncoder.WriteStructuredAppend`, so each symbol is otherwise exactly the stream `Create` writes for its chunk; one symbol is `Create` itself, byte-identical. Charset once from the whole text, forced on every chunk; parity once over the whole text's bytes in that charset, the byte order mark included when the first chunk writes one; the boost decided for the set at the shared version; mask, quiet zone and segmentation per symbol; splits snapped past a low surrogate. `StructuredAppendEncodeTest` (21 cases through the 5a decoder: round trips per mode and charset, the one-symbol collapse compared module for module with `Create`, the sixteen-symbol ceiling and the seventeenth's `ArgumentException`, parity per charset and with a BOM, surrogate pairs, mask, quiet zone, uniform boost, `Optimal` never needing more symbols, a forced ECI on ASCII, empty text, an uncapped range, an exact version, a character that fits no symbol, and the contradictory options `Create` refuses) and `StructuredAppendPlannerTest` (15 cases: the three minimality properties against an independent one-character-at-a-time greedy walk on seven texts, the empty and refused cases, and the parity against `Encoding` for each charset and for a lone surrogate). Full suite green on both target frameworks: 9,943 on net10.0, 9,930 on net8.0. The encoder spec gains a scope row and a section, the migration guide an encode section, the shared spec its "read and written" sentence; listing and Playground page regenerated.

**The version cap is the count parameter, and it makes the search cheap.** With the cap as the only input, the split is three searches over the symbol count, and the count is at most sixteen; no capacity model beyond the one the single-symbol path already has was needed, because each chunk's cost is what `Create` would charge for it plus the two headers.

**Cost had to be monotone for any of this to be a binary search, and it is, in both models.** A longer prefix never plans cheaper under the mixed-mode dynamic program (a plan for the longer prefix restricted to the shorter is a plan for the shorter at no more cost) and never costs less in single mode (each mode step widens per-character cost). The surrogate snap keeps that: snapping an end past a low surrogate is monotone in the end, so the predicate stays monotone through it.

**Two edges the first draft missed, both found by tests.** An empty text produced zero chunks and an empty set (the walk never runs), where the design says one plain symbol; and the parity helper reached for `Encoding` span overloads that netstandard2.0 does not have, which the four-framework core build refused, so the parity is now a per-code-point UTF-8 XOR with no encoder and no buffer, and it mirrors the writer's U+FFFD for a lone surrogate.

**Benchmark delta.** The single-symbol encode path gained one predictable branch in each data writer (`if (!config.StructuredAppend.IsEmpty)`) and 12 bytes on the configuration record it passes by reference. `SimpleEncode` (FeatherQR category, default job, `e93a3d3` in a worktree against this tree, sequential runs, nothing else running): Number 829.3 → 820.8 ns, Alphanumeric 1,127.9 → 1,120.4, Url 1,312.6 → 1,404.3, Unicode 1,347.4 → 1,434.5, Wifi 1,222.9 → 1,245.7; allocations identical (120 / 144 / 176 / 208 / 176 B). Every case is inside the +10 % rule, and a `--job short` pass beforehand moved Url and Wifi the other way (−0.4 % and −5 %), so the spread is the machine's, not the branch's. `CreateStructuredAppend` itself is a new path and has no baseline; it allocates the result array and one `QRCodeData` per symbol, and nothing else the single-symbol path does not.

### Phase 5c, interop (2026-09-15)

**Done.** Two checks, one permanent and one by hand. `StructuredAppendZXingCrossTest` (nine sets covering every charset, `Optimal`, the boost, a byte order mark and the sixteen-symbol set) has an independent in-process reader read each symbol this library writes and requires the position, count, parity and text to equal what this library's own decoder reports; it runs in CI. The tool's `spot-check-structured-append` widens that to the three pinned readers, two of them from a rendered luminance image and one from the module matrix, over the seven corpus texts and five option variants: 33 sets, **196 symbols, 196/196 agreement on every reader**, and the parity byte-identical with the pinned balancing encoder's for the same text and level on all **21** comparable combinations. The findings are in the fixture spec's oracle matrix. Decode-side interop was already the 5a corpus (95 third-party symbols plus 4 captures).

**Two things the check taught, both about the check.** A parity comparison is only meaningful when both encoders chose the same charset: forcing UTF-8 on the Latin-1 text yields 8 where the oracle's ISO-8859-1 set carries 139, both correct, so the tool compares only the variants where both pick the charset from the text. And the independent reader keeps a byte order mark in its text where this library's decoder consumes it, so a text comparison across readers has to trim it; the header fields need no such care.

**Benchmark delta.** Not measured: no production code changed; a test and a tool command.

### Performance round 1, the searches stop where they cannot win (2026-09-15)

**Done.** A performance review of 5b, before this round, put a `QRCodeStructuredAppendEncode` benchmark beside the segmentation one: its baseline arm encodes the chunks of the split one `Create` each at the set's version, so the Ratio column is the planning overhead itself. It read 83x (Single) and 1,240x (Optimal) on 45,000 ASCII characters into sixteen version 40 symbols on the open range, and 6.9x / 137x with the version pinned: the version scan was most of the feature's cost, and the reason was that the greedy walk never stopped. Asked whether a low version holds sixteen chunks, it split the whole text into thousands, each with a binary search over the remaining text. Two changes, both in `StructuredAppendPlanner`: the walk takes the count it is asked about and returns past it as soon as it is exceeded; and a lower bound on what any split can cost (each character at the cheapest rate any mode gives it, plus the headers every symbol pays at the narrowest widths any version has, `CheapestPayloadBits` and `CanHold`) is priced once and gates every search, so a version whose capacity times the count cannot reach it is not walked, and the budget search starts at the bound's average share instead of at one bit. The bound only rejects; the walk still decides. `StructuredAppendPlannerTest` gains three tests (18 cases): the bound never refuses a count the walk reaches, at every version and level over the seven texts; it does refuse one no split can reach; and the limited walk returns the reference walk's count and chunk ends within the limit and a value past it beyond. The split itself is unchanged, which the existing minimality properties pin. Full suite green on both target frameworks (19,899 cases). The encoder spec's Structured Append section gains the paragraph.

**Lessons.** A walk that answers a yes/no question has nothing to learn after the first no, and a search that cannot win still costs (the rMQR planner's lesson, again). The bound had to be additive over chunks to bound a set, and it is only because a split never cuts a surrogate pair. Writing the bound's exactness as a test against the walk it gates, rather than reasoning it, is what made it safe to put in front of every search.

**Benchmark delta.** `QRCodeStructuredAppendEncode`, ShortRun, sequential runs on this tree before and after, nothing else running. Mean per op, before → after (Ratio to the Symbols arm): byte-45k-any Single 95.0 → 6.4 ms (83x → 6.4x), Optimal 1,413 → 81 ms (1,240x → 81x); byte-45k-v40 Single 7.2 → 5.5 ms, Optimal 142 → 99 ms; byte-4k-max10 Single 1.21 → 0.32 ms (22x → 6.3x), Optimal 30.5 → 7.3 ms (565x → 145x); mixed-40k-any Single 67.3 → 7.2 ms, Optimal 1,521 → 138 ms; numeric-100k-any Single 74.8 → 4.4 ms, Optimal 2,887 → 232 ms; utf8-15k-any Single 9.6 → 1.36 ms (11.6x → 1.4x), Optimal 992 → 25 ms. Allocations unchanged on every row. What remains on the Single rows is the per-probe re-analysis of over-long prefixes, and on the Optimal rows the dynamic program running on every probe, all-digit chunks included; both are recorded in the review and are the next rounds.

### Performance round 2, the chunk end without pricing whole prefixes (2026-09-15)

**Done.** Round 1 left the walk finding each chunk end by a binary search whose every probe priced a prefix from scratch, with a full text analysis and, under `Optimal`, a full cost run, over a prefix that could reach the end of the text. `LongestChunkEnd` now finds the end in one step. In single mode a prefix's mode changes at most twice along the text (Numeric, then Alphanumeric, then Byte, each boundary the first character outside the narrower alphabet), and within a mode the cost is a closed form of the length, so the end is a few arithmetic steps (`MostNumeric`, `MostAlphanumeric`, a byte quotient) plus, for a UTF-8 Byte run, one pass over the run's own bytes with the writer's per-code-point sizes, pairs kept whole. Under `Optimal` the mixed plan holds the single-mode plan among its candidates, so its cost decides, and `ModeSegmenter.LongestPrefixWithinBudget` runs the segmentation program forward once: the optimum of every prefix falls out of the sweep and is monotone in the length, so it stops at the first prefix over budget. It is skipped inside an all-digit run, which no split improves, and narrowed to the leading alphanumeric run behind a byte order mark, which only a Byte-mode chunk carries; the window is capped at the most any symbol holds, so no prefix longer than a chunk can be is ever priced. The program's per-character step moved into `ModeSegmenter.Advance`, shared by `ComputeCosts` and the forward walk, so there is still one cost model. `ChunkBits` stays as the definition, and is what the tests hold the fast path to: `ModeSegmenterPrefixBudgetTest` (11 cases) prices every prefix with `ComputeCosts` and takes the last within budget, on every budget the answer can turn on, across the three count indicator bands; `StructuredAppendPlannerTest.LongestChunkEnd_MatchesTheReferenceWalk` (25 cases: nine texts, both segmentations, the byte order mark on the UTF-8 ones) does the same against the one-character-at-a-time reference walk at three versions and three starts. Full suite green on both target frameworks.

**Two defects, both caught by the parity tests rather than by review.** The first cut handed the forward program the budget with the mode indicator already subtracted, though the program prices each run's indicator itself; every `Optimal` case tripped the assertion that a plan never fits less than the single-mode stream. The second was narrower and was found by reading the fast path against the definition afterwards: a byte order mark suppressed the plan for the whole chunk, where `ChunkBits` suppresses it only once the chunk is Byte mode, which is what actually carries the mark. A first chunk that stays inside the alphanumeric alphabet carries none, so under `Optimal` with `Utf8Bom` on a UTF-8 set, a leading alphanumeric run a split makes cheaper was cut short and the set could come out with more symbols than it needs. Never an invalid symbol, since a shorter chunk always fits, which is why nothing else noticed. The plan is now searched over that leading run alone, and `alnumDigitsThenJapanese` (an alphanumeric-and-digit prefix in a UTF-8 text) pins it: restoring the old line fails exactly those two cases and nothing else.

**Lessons.** The cost of a prefix is not something to recompute per probe when it is a closed form of the length, or falls out of a sweep the program already makes. A fast path that must agree with a definition needs the definition kept beside it, and a test that tries every budget the answer can turn on; a handful of round-trip tests would have passed both slips for a long time. And a divergence that only loses optimality, never correctness, is invisible to every test that checks the output decodes, so it has to be checked against the definition directly.

**Benchmark delta.** `QRCodeStructuredAppendEncode`, ShortRun, sequential runs on this tree before and after. Mean per op, before → after (Ratio to the Symbols arm): byte-45k-any Single 6.35 → 1.23 ms (6.4x → 1.25x), Optimal 80.7 → 8.3 ms (81x → 8.5x); byte-45k-v40 Single 5.45 → 1.17 ms, Optimal 99.1 → 7.6 ms; byte-4k-max10 Single 318 → 62 us (6.3x → 1.1x), Optimal 7.26 → 0.44 ms (145x → 7.7x); mixed-40k-any Single 7.19 → 0.81 ms (9.4x → 1.02x), Optimal 138 → 13.7 ms (180x → 17x); numeric-100k-any Single 4.41 → 1.65 ms (4.4x → 1.6x), Optimal 232 → 3.3 ms (229x → 3.2x); utf8-15k-any Single 1.36 → 0.99 ms (1.4x → 1.2x), Optimal 25.1 → 2.9 ms (25x → 3.5x). Allocations unchanged on every row. The Single arms now sit within 2 to 60 % of the symbols alone; what remains there is the version and budget searches themselves, and on the `Optimal` arms the forward program still runs once per chunk per search step over prose no split can improve.

The `ModeSegmenter` extraction is the one part of this round that other callers share, so it was measured on its own: `QRCodeSegmentationEncode`, ShortRun, two passes per side alternating between a worktree at the previous commit and this tree, best of two. Every row is within noise and none regresses beyond it. The widest move against is `byte-120` Optimal at +5.9 %, on a pass whose `byte-120` Single arm, which never enters the segmenter, moved +2.0 % with it; the widest move for is `mixed-120` Optimal at −20 %, on a pass whose `mixed-20` Single arm moved −11 %. Taking the Single arms as the machine's own spread, ±11 % is what these benchmarks resolve, and the refactor sits inside it.

### Performance round 3, one rule for the content no plan can help (2026-09-16)

**Done.** The two rounds before this left a cost run still happening on content the version scan had always known to skip: all-Numeric. No mode prices a digit below Numeric and every extra run adds a header, so one Numeric run is the optimum and a plan can only match it. The scan had that rule inline; the Structured Append chunk cost and the per-symbol writer did not, so a set of digits ran the dynamic program once per chunk in `CreateSymbol`, with its parents table and reconstruction, and once per chunk per level the ECC boost tried in `EveryChunkFits`. The rule is now `QRSegmentPlanner.CanPlanBeatSingleMode`, one predicate the three of them ask, carrying the reason and the warning that a caller answering it with no skips a whole cost run. Round 2's chunk-end walk needs no change: its prefix-wise form of the same rule, ending the walk inside a leading digit run, was already there. `QRSegmentPlannerUnitTest` pins the rule two ways (the program's own cost for digits equals one run, at every band, both charsets and the lengths that land mid packing group; and the predicate is Numeric only), and `StructuredAppendEncodeTest` pins that a digit set under `Optimal` is the single-mode set module for module, with and without the boost. Full suite green on both target frameworks (19,981 cases). The encoder spec's "Content that cannot benefit" paragraph now names the three callers.

**The benchmark had no boost row, so half of this was unmeasurable.** `BoostEccLevel` is in the feature's option table and was in none of the eight shapes, though it is the option that re-costs every chunk up to three more times. Two shapes were added, prose and digits with the boost on, and the baseline arm now encodes its symbols at the level the set actually came out at, read back from the decoder in the setup, so a boosted row's Ratio still means the planning overhead and nothing else.

**Lessons.** A rule stated inline in one caller is a rule the next caller will not know about; naming it is what let the two that had missed it ask. And an option that no benchmark row turns on is an option whose cost nobody knows: the boost had been shipped, specified and tested for correctness, and was still invisible here.

**Benchmark delta.** `QRCodeStructuredAppendEncode`, ShortRun, two passes per side alternating between a worktree at the previous commit and this tree, best of two. The two digit rows move and nothing else does: numeric-100k-any Optimal 3.03 → 1.27 ms (−58 %), numeric-100k-boost Optimal 3.41 → 1.34 ms (−61 %). Both now sit level with their own Single arm (1.42x and 1.43x of the symbols alone, against 1.38x and 1.40x for Single), which is the point: planning digits now costs what not planning them costs. Every other row is inside the machine's spread, which this run showed to be wide, as the untouched Symbols arms moved between −24 % and +0.1 % on their own. Allocations unchanged. What remains is `mixed-40k-any` at 17x and `byte-45k-*` at 7 to 9x, where the forward program runs once per chunk per search step on content that genuinely could be split; narrowing that is a different change from this one.

### Performance round 4, the charset the analysis already chose (2026-09-16)

**Done.** `TextAnalyzer` classifies the text in one pass, deciding among other things whether every `char` fits a single byte, and then threw that answer away: the Byte-mode data length re-derived it with `CharacterSets.IsValidISO88591`, a second scan, and handed the text to an `Encoding` for a third. The classification's own flag is passed to the count now, and the count needs no pass at all except for UTF-8, because Latin-1 is one byte per `char`. That last part was worth establishing rather than assuming, since it is what the whole shortcut rests on: the writer narrows each `char`, and the encoder replaces each `char` it cannot represent with one byte of its own, a surrogate pair counting as the two code units it is rather than the one scalar it spells, which a probe confirmed (`Encoding.GetEncoding("ISO-8859-1").GetByteCount("🎉")` is 2, not 1). So the count and the bytes written agree for every input, including a charset the caller forced over content it cannot represent, and the `Encoding` call and the netstandard2.0 `ToString()` behind it are both gone. `TextAnalyzerByteCountTest` (90 cases) pins the data length against `Encoding` per charset and content class, and pins that a forced Latin-1 symbol is still one a reader takes apart, one char back per char in. The existing tier parity tests already compare whole `TextAnalysisResult` values, so the new flag is covered on every SIMD tier for free. Full suite green on both target frameworks (20,071 cases).

**A mutation that survived is what found the real shape of this.** Replacing the forced-Latin-1 branch with a bare `text.Length` was meant to fail a test and did not, and the reason was not a gap in the corpus: the two are equal, always, on every input. The branch existed to defer to an encoder that had nothing to add, and deleting it makes the count provably equal to what the writer emits on both target framework families rather than incidentally equal on one. A mutation that survives is worth reading before it is worth patching.

**Benchmark delta.** `SimpleEncode`, ShortRun, one pass per side against a worktree at the previous commit; the second pass was abandoned because the machine had stopped being quiet. Read with the rows the change cannot reach as the control: Number +1.1 % and Alphanumeric −0.5 % (both count characters, not bytes, so neither ever entered this code), against Url −5.2 % and Wifi −7.0 % (ASCII Byte mode, which lost both extra passes) and Unicode −2.0 % (UTF-8, which lost the redundant scan but still has to be counted). The ordering is what the change predicts and the controls are tight, but it is one pass: the third-party rows in the same table moved between −14 % and +30 %, and the version 40 rows of `QRCodeEncodeEndToEnd` are dominated by error correction and placement, so nothing there resolves a change of this size. The allocation this removes is netstandard2.0-only, where every Byte-mode analysis copied the text to a string, so no benchmark here shows it.

### Performance round 5, work the set does once instead of per symbol (2026-09-16)

**Done.** Three pieces of repeated work, each small, all in the path from a finished plan to the symbols. The ECC boost asked every chunk whether it fits the next level, once per level it tried, though a chunk's cost does not depend on the level at all: the set is priced once now and each level compares its capacity against the fullest chunk, so a boost that climbs to H costs one pricing pass instead of four, and a set that is not boosted pays for none, as before. `CreateSymbol` analysed its chunk two or three times, once for itself, once inside the configuration it built, and once more to re-price the single-mode stream for the guard that catches a chunk the planner mis-fitted; it analyses once now, builds the configuration from that analysis directly, and prices the guard through `StructuredAppendPlanner.SingleModeChunkBits`, which is the half of `ChunkBits` that does not need the text. And the matrix work buffer and the mixed-mode plan buffer were taken per symbol although every symbol of a set shares the version that sizes them; both are taken once for the set, the plan buffer sized to the longest chunk, which also decides the stack-or-pool question once rather than sixteen times. `StructuredAppendEncodeTest` gains a boost that climbs more than one level (a pinned version whose symbols each fill about half of it, both segmentations), which is the walk the first piece changes and which no test had reached: the existing boost test sits on a tight fit where the first level up already fails. Full suite green on both target frameworks (20,075 cases).

**Both risky pieces were mutation-checked, because neither changes what the library emits.** Pricing the last chunk instead of the fullest fails the existing uniform-boost test; dropping the three Byte-mode units a byte order mark adds fails the existing mark test. A refactor whose whole point is that the output does not move needs to be shown that the output would move if it were done wrong.

**Lessons.** A value that does not depend on the loop variable does not belong inside the loop, and "is this level small enough" had the shape of a question about the level when it was a question about the set. The benchmark shapes added for the boost in round 3 turned out not to exercise the climb at all, because a balanced split at L leaves no room to reach M: a shape that turns an option on is not the same as a shape that makes the option work, and only writing the test that climbs made that visible.

**Benchmark delta.** Not resolved. `QRCodeStructuredAppendEncode`, one pass per side against a worktree at the previous commit, could not separate this change from the machine, which by then had been running benchmarks and test suites for hours: the `Symbols` arms, which this change does not touch at all, moved between −53 % and +18 % on their own, and no row of the set moved further than that. What the change removes is countable rather than measured here: two of the three text analyses each symbol did, so about 90,000 fewer characters scanned for a sixteen-symbol set of 45,000; a boost that climbs three levels pricing the set once instead of four times; and one buffer rental per set in place of sixteen. Allocations are unchanged. Re-measuring on an idle machine is the honest way to put a number on it, and is worth doing before the row is quoted anywhere.

### Performance round 6, the bracket the balanced budget is searched in (2026-09-16)

**Done.** Counting rather than timing located the cost, which is what the loaded machine had stopped being able to do. A counter in the segmentation program says how many characters it steps over per plan, and the answer for a sixteen-symbol set of 45,000 was 740,000, about sixteen passes over the whole text; three of the four shapes that ran it came out byte-identical to the single-mode set, so most of that bought nothing. The passes are the probes of the third search, the one for the smallest per-symbol budget: a probe walks the text into chunks and each chunk costs a forward pass of the program, so the search costs one pass per bisection step and the number of steps is the log of the bracket it starts with.

**The bracket was thousands of bits wide around an answer tens of bits from one end.** The floor came from pricing every character at the cheapest rate any mode could give it, which calls a lowercase letter five and a half bits, and on prose that sits nearly two thousand bits under the truth. The ceiling was the version's whole data capacity, a thousand bits above it, and measuring showed that side dominated: tightening only the floor moved prose by six per cent, cost `utf8-15k-any` eight per cent and put a whole wasted pass back on the all-digit shape that round 3 had cleared. Both ends are computed now, each from one pass over the text: below, the minimal plan for the whole text divided by the count, since the plans of a split concatenate into one for the whole and so cost at least it; above, the fullest chunk of the text cut into equal character counts, since that is itself a split into this many chunks and therefore a budget that already holds them. Two passes replace six or seven. They are taken only where a probe is itself a pass, so `Single` and content no plan can beat (the rule round 3 named) keep the cheap bounds and pay nothing.

`StructuredAppendPlannerTest.Budget_IsTheSmallestThatHoldsTheCount` is the guard the whole change rests on: over ten texts, both segmentations and all four levels, the budget holds the count and one bit below it does not. Raising the floor above the answer fails it in six cases, and a ceiling taken from the emptiest chunk instead of the fullest fails it too, so neither bound can go unsound quietly. Full suite green on both target frameworks (20,095 cases).

**Lessons.** When timing stops resolving anything, count something instead: the counter found both the size of the waste and which end of the bracket it was at, on a machine too busy to time a thing. And a bound is worth tightening only where it is loose, which is a measurement, not an intuition: the first cut of this tightened the end that was already tight, and the corpus said so immediately.

**Benchmark delta.** Deterministic, since these are counted operations rather than elapsed time: characters the segmentation program steps over per plan, before then after. `byte-45k-v40` 651,895 → 401,506 (−38 %), `byte-45k-any` 739,991 → 489,602 (−34 %), `mixed-40k-any` 895,647 → 669,938 (−25 %), `utf8-15k-any` 203,042 → 163,688 (−19 %), `byte-4k-max10` 42,380 → 35,537 (−16 %), `numeric-100k-any` 0 → 0. In passes over the text, `byte-45k-v40` goes from 14.5 to 8.9 and `mixed-40k-any` from 22.4 to 16.7. No shape regresses. Wall-clock was not re-measured, because the machine had been under load for hours and its untouched control rows were moving by half; the ratio this should show is roughly the same fraction off the planning share of the `Optimal` rows.

### Performance round 7, not consulting the program about content it cannot help (2026-09-16)

**Done.** The counting from round 6 had already said the uncomfortable part out loud: of the shapes that ran the segmentation program, three produced a set byte-identical to the single-mode one, so every pass they paid bought nothing. What decides that is cheap to know. A plan is only cheaper than one run when some run of it is in a mode denser than the whole content's, and such a run has to repay at least the one mode indicator and count indicator it adds, which at the narrowest band means four digits or six characters of the alphanumeric alphabet. English prose holds neither: its longest alphanumeric stretch is three, a full stop, a space and the next capital. So one pass for the longest run of each denser mode, taken over the whole text since no chunk's runs are longer than it, answers whether any chunk's plan can beat its single-mode stream, and when the answer is no the three searches run as `Single` and never touch the program. The split is the same split, because the two costs are the same number.

The per-symbol writer is deliberately left alone. There, `TryBuildPlan` reconstructs some minimal plan, and when the minimum is a tie the plan it picks is not always the single run; skipping it on this rule would change which of two equally priced streams a symbol carries, where skipping it in the searches provably cannot. That is the one pass per set that remains.

`PlanCouldWinTest` is the guard, and it is the whole of the argument: over content built with a run of each denser mode at every length from zero to twenty-two, at the start, the middle and the end and alone, across the three count indicator bands and both charsets, whenever the predicate says no the program must agree that no plan is cheaper. 712 cases. Full suite green on both target frameworks (20,807 cases).

**Lessons.** The cheapest question to ask about an optimisation is whether its answer can differ from the default at all, and it took counting to notice that for most content it cannot. The thresholds are a break-even, so they belong in the code as derived constants with the arithmetic beside them, the way the segment planner's own bounds already do. And the test had two bugs before the code had any: an alphanumeric run counted by eye, and a cost run asked about a charset the text had not been analysed under, which prices Japanese as one byte per character.

**Benchmark delta.** Counted, not timed: characters the segmentation program steps over per plan, round 6 then now. `byte-45k-any` 489,602 → 45,000 (−91 %), `byte-45k-v40` 401,506 → 45,000 (−89 %), `utf8-15k-any` 163,688 → 15,000 (−91 %), `byte-4k-max10` 35,537 → 4,000 (−89 %), `mixed-40k-any` 669,938 unchanged, `numeric-100k-any` 0 unchanged. What is left on the shapes that moved is exactly one pass, which is the per-symbol writer and nothing else; the searches no longer step over a character. `mixed-40k-any` keeps every pass it had, which is the point: its digit runs are ten long, a plan does win, and the predicate says so. Across the two rounds the shapes that cannot benefit from planning went from about sixteen passes over the text to one.

### Performance round 8, the runs only Byte encodes (2026-09-16)

**Done.** Rounds 6 and 7 removed passes; this one makes the passes that remain cheaper, and it is the only round whose gain is per character rather than per pass. The segmentation program carries seven states, but a character outside the alphanumeric alphabet can only extend a Byte run, so one such character leaves every other state unreachable and they stay that way until an alphanumeric one arrives. Both loops notice that and take the step as one addition to the Byte state plus the predecessor the state machine would have written, instead of clearing seven states, relaxing from seven and copying seven back. Digits are alphanumeric, so one class test per character answers both questions and the numeric test inside the step is now reached only when it can be true.

Where the characters are, measured by counting them: 86 % of the program's steps on Japanese behind a UTF-8 declaration, 55 % on English prose, 24 % on the digit-and-word mixture, which is the shape that still runs the program sixteen times. `ModeSegmenter` is shared by all three symbologies, so the guard is a parity test rather than an end-to-end one: `ModeSegmenterByteRunParityTest` puts an independent program beside it, one that always walks all seven states and shares only the cost model's numbers, and holds the two together on cost, final state and the reconstructed plan over seventeen texts built around long Byte runs, boundaries and surrogates, across the three count indicator bands, three charsets and the mode-availability flags Micro QR passes. Letting the fast path trigger after an alphanumeric character fails it on six of them. Full suite green on both target frameworks (20,875 cases).

**Lessons.** An optimisation whose gain is per character cannot be measured by the counter that found the last two rounds, so it needs its own number, and "what fraction of the steps does it take" is that number. It is also the round where the shared code finally had to be treated as shared: the two rounds before it lived in the Structured Append planner, this one is under Micro QR and rMQR as well, which is what makes an independent reference the right guard rather than a corpus.

**Benchmark delta.** Not resolved, and the run says so plainly: every `Optimal` row moved with its `Single` partner, which never enters the program, and `numeric-100k-any` `Single`, which enters nothing this touches, moved −45 %. The machine had been running benchmarks for most of a day. What is established without it is the share of steps the fast path takes, above, and what a step costs on each side: one addition and one store against a seven-state clear, a seven-way relax and a seven-state copy. The broadest beneficiary is not measured here at all, since `ComputeCosts` is what the single-symbol `Optimal` path and both other symbologies' planners run; `QRCodeSegmentationEncode`, `RmQRSegmentationEncode` and `MicroQRSegmentationEncode` are where that would show, on a quiet machine.

### Re-measurement of rounds 6 to 8 on a quiet machine (2026-09-17)

**What was measured.** Wall-clock for the three structural rounds together, which the loaded machine had not been able to resolve: a worktree at the commit before round 6 against this tree, ShortRun, each benchmark class run on one side and then the other back to back so the two sides of a class are minutes apart rather than half an hour. Controls held this time: the `Symbols` and `Single` arms mostly moved within a few per cent.

**`QRCodeStructuredAppendEncode`, `Optimal` arms, before → after (Ratio to the symbols alone).** `byte-45k-any` 7.86 → 1.30 ms (8.35x → 1.33x, −83 %); `byte-45k-boost` 8.14 → 1.58 ms (8.45x → 1.75x, −81 %); `byte-45k-v40` 6.91 → 1.52 ms (7.07x → 1.60x, −78 %); `byte-4k-max10` 430 → 76 us (8.51x → 1.58x, −82 %); `utf8-15k-any` 2.89 → 1.07 ms (−63 %; its ratio is not quoted because that run's `Symbols` arm moved +52 % on its own); `mixed-40k-any` 13.36 → 9.96 ms (16.87x → 12.84x, −25 %); the digit shapes unchanged within noise, as they had no program run to remove. `Single` arms flat. Allocations unchanged.

**The shared program, measured where it is shared.** Round 8 is the only one of the three that reaches outside Structured Append. `RmQRSegmentationEncode` shows it where rMQR plans digit-and-letter content: `mixed-120` −18 %, `alt10-120` −20 %, `mixed-150` −9 %, `Single` arms flat. `QRCodeSegmentationEncode` moves with its `Single` arms (both −2 % to −6 %), since the Standard QR version scan rarely runs the program at all. The fast path is not free where it never engages: content that alternates every character pays the extra class test and bookkeeping for nothing, `alt1-120` +5.5 % on Standard QR and +2.6 % on rMQR, and Micro QR's eight- and nineteen-character mixtures +4 % to +6 %, all inside the +10 % rule. One first-pass reading of `byte-120` at +20 % carried a standard deviation of 495 ns against 15 ns before; a second pass on both sides put it at +1 %, best of two.

**Lessons.** The counted reductions of rounds 6 and 7 translated into wall-clock almost one to one on the shapes they targeted, which is what makes counting a fair stand-in on a loaded machine; the per-step gain of round 8 did not have that luxury and needed the quiet run to show, and showed its cost as well as its gain.

### Performance round 9, the version scan on content a plan does help (2026-09-17)

**Done.** With rounds 6 to 8 in, `mixed-40k-any` under `Optimal` was the one shape still paying for the segmentation program many times over, 16.7 passes over the text, and counting them by phase moved the target: the budget search was down to five walks over a 26-bit bracket, but the version scan was walking eight versions below the answer (v39) and running each walk nearly to the end of the text before it could say fourteen chunks do not fit, 6.8 passes on its own. The gate in front of the scan is the rate bound from round 1, which prices every digit as if it sat in a full Numeric group, and on digit-and-word content that sits about 7,500 bits under the truth. Under `Optimal`, a version the rate bound admits is now checked against the minimal plan for the whole text at that version's count indicator widths (`CanHoldPlanned`): the chunks' plans concatenate into one plan for the whole at the same widths, so they cost at least it between them, and each chunk also pays its headers. For this text that floor is about 311,600 bits; version 38-L offers 14 × (21,616 − 20) = 302,344 and is turned away, version 39-L offers 314,664 and is walked. The floor is computed once per count indicator band and shared with the budget bracket, which needed the same number already. `Single` is untouched, since its walks are arithmetic.

`StructuredAppendPlannerTest` gains three tests (18 cases): the planned floor never refuses a count the walk reaches, at every version and level, over nine texts under `Optimal` and one under `Single`; it does turn away versions the rate bound admits on mixed content, each confirmed by the walk; and, with the walk alone and no bound, every version below the chosen one fails to hold the count. Loosening the floor by 2,000 bits fails eighteen soundness cases and two version cases, the latter being a set actually placed at a larger version. Full suite green on both target frameworks (20,909 cases).

**Lessons.** A bound that was tight enough when the walks behind it were cheap stops being tight enough once each walk is a pass; the gate needed to be as exact as the thing it guards was expensive. And the phase that dominates moves as the others are fixed: round 6 made the search cheap, which is what made the scan worth counting.

**Benchmark delta.** Counted, characters the program steps over per plan: `mixed-40k-any` 669,938 → 436,998 (−35 %, 16.7 → 10.9 passes); one pass more than the scan's share predicted, spent on the floor for a band below the answer whose candidates the rate bound admitted. `mixed-4k-max10`, an extra probe capped at version 10, 42,693 → 39,691 (−7 %), where two bands' floors are paid. Every other shape unchanged, with the same version and symbol count. Timed, `QRCodeStructuredAppendEncode`, ShortRun, the previous commit's worktree then this tree back to back: `mixed-40k-any` `Optimal` 10.27 → 7.39 ms (12.59x → 8.99x, −28 %), its `Symbols` arm +0.8 %; the other `Optimal` rows within −10 % to +2 %. One unrelated outlier, `byte-45k-boost` `Single` +50 %, on a path this change does not reach.

### Performance round 10, not walking the answer twice (2026-09-17)

**Done.** The budget search ended by walking the text once more at the budget it had just found, to fill the caller's chunk ends. That walk had already happened: the probe that last lowered the ceiling walked at exactly that budget, since the search ends with the floor meeting the ceiling it set. Its split is now kept aside as it succeeds, because every later probe that fails overwrites the caller's buffer on its way to failing, and handed back at the end. The text is walked a final time only when no probe lowered the ceiling at all, which is when the bracket's own ceiling was already the answer; the even-cut ceiling is a budget, not a greedy split, so its cut points cannot stand in for the walk.

`StructuredAppendPlannerTest.Plan_ChunkEnds_AreTheWalkAtTheReturnedBudget` (20 cases: ten texts, both segmentations, all four levels, and version ranges pinned at 10, 27 and 40 as well as open, which is what puts some answers at the top of the bracket) requires the split handed back to equal a fresh walk at the budget handed back. Not copying the kept split back fails 28 cases; not walking when nothing settled the answer fails six, so both paths are reached. Replacing the check `settledBudget == low` with `settledBudget >= 0` fails nothing, and correctly so: once any probe succeeds, the loop's invariant makes the two the same condition. Full suite green on both target frameworks (20,929 cases).

**Lessons.** A mutation that survives because it is equivalent is still worth running, since reading why it survived is what confirms the invariant the code rests on; the useful follow-up was a different mutation on the path the first one could not reach.

**Benchmark delta.** Counted, characters the program steps over per plan: `mixed-40k-any` 436,998 → 396,985 (−9 %, 10.9 → 9.9 passes), exactly the final walk; `mixed-4k-max10` unchanged at 39,691, one of the cases the bracket's ceiling is the answer; every other shape unchanged. Timed, `QRCodeStructuredAppendEncode`, ShortRun, the previous commit's worktree then this tree: `mixed-40k-any` `Optimal` 7.12 → 6.23 ms (−13 %), but its `Symbols` and `Single` arms moved −9 % and −7 % in the same direction on paths this change does not reach, and its Ratio went 8.51x → 8.02x (−6 %); the counted −9 % sits between the two readings and is the number to quote. The other rows' controls moved between −22 % and +12 % in this run, so nothing smaller than that is read from it.

### Performance round 11, the program's step in registers (2026-09-17)

**Done.** Rounds 6 to 10 cut the passes; this one cuts the pass. Measured per phase, `mixed-40k-any` under `Optimal` was 10 passes of the segmentation program at 13 ns per character, 5.1 ms of planning over 0.78 ms of symbols, and the program's step was the cost: seven states relaxed from seven through two stack arrays, a bounds-checked write per relaxation, a 28-byte copy per character and, on the prefix walk, a scan of the six states per character. `ModeSegmenter` now keeps the six costs in locals and computes each target as the cheaper of continuing its run or opening it from the cheapest state, one add and one min; a Latin charset with Byte allowed has its own loop for costs, for costs with parents and for the prefix walk (the constant byte cost and the mode flags decided once, not per character), UTF-8 and the Micro QR versions without a mode share one general loop per entry point, every loop steps a run outside the alphanumeric alphabet as one add per character (round 8's rule, in register form), the prefix walk derives its answer from where it stopped instead of writing an end per character, and on a Latin symbol the six parents of a character are one 8-byte store. Where parents are recorded the candidates are tried in state order and replaced only when strictly cheaper, the tie-break the relaxation had, so the plans reconstruct byte for byte. The one-character class comes from a 128-entry table. Tried and refuted on the way, each with its reason in the spec: a vector form of the step, a branch-free minimum, and a factored recurrence. `ModeSegmenterPlanParityTest` (three tests, 47 texts including seeded random mixes of every class, three charsets, five width sets including the Micro QR shapes, all four mode-availability combinations) holds every loop to the all-states relaxation with its predecessor rule on cost, final state, the reconstructed runs and the walk's stopping point at every budget it can turn on, and pins the class table to `CharacterSets` for every char. Full suite green on both target frameworks (10,575 on net10.0, 10,562 on net8.0), the existing parity and prefix-budget tests untouched and passing.

**Lessons.** The 13 ns were memory, not arithmetic: registerising the state alone was 4x, before any instruction-level idea. The minimums compile to compare-and-branch, not conditional moves, and the predictor learns which candidate wins because that is decided by the structure of the costs rather than the content; so the two ideas that assume a serial chain (shortening it, and removing the branches) both lost, and the vector form lost because its horizontal minimum and broadcast are a longer chain than the scalar one. Measure the parents-recording path separately from the cost-only path: the first register form was 3x on the walks and 27 % slower on the UTF-8 writer, because the fast path for byte runs had been left out of the tracking loop. And a benchmark harness whose correctness gate calls the baseline far more often than the variants skews tiered PGO's profile of the baseline; a byte-identical canary showed the reference running 25 to 50 % slower than its copy, and moving the gate's reference to the canary fixed it.

**Benchmark delta.** Kernel, `Optimal` shapes, per character: the walk 12.8 → 2.0 ns (6.5x), the whole-text plan 11.0 → 2.0 (5.5x), the per-symbol plan with parents 11.2 → 3.0 on digit-and-word content (3.75x), 4.2 → 1.6 on prose, 3.6 → 1.7 on Japanese behind UTF-8. End to end, ShortRun, a worktree at the previous commit then this tree, each class back to back: `QRCodeStructuredAppendEncode` `mixed-40k-any` `Optimal` 6.76 → 2.42 ms (7.80x → 2.86x, −64 %), `byte-45k-any` `Optimal` 1.67 → 1.37 ms (−18 %), `byte-4k-max10` `Optimal` 87.7 → 74.3 us (−15 %), `utf8-15k-any` and the digit shapes within noise; one control outlier, `byte-45k-any` `Single` +100 % on a path the program never runs, beside `byte-45k-boost` `Single` −25 % on the same path. The shared program elsewhere: `QRCodeSegmentationEncode` `mixed-1000` 52.0 → 28.8 us (−45 %), `mixed-120` −42 %, `url-58` −39 %, `alt1-120` −28 %; `RmQRSegmentationEncode` `alt10-120` −55 %, `mixed-150` −51 %, `mixed-120` −51 %, `url-38` −39 %, `utf8-60` −44 %; `MicroQRSegmentationEncode` `mixed-19` 1,082 → 399 ns (−63 %), `mixed-8` −38 %. The alphanumeric-only shapes moved +3 to +5 % on all three symbologies (200 ns to 2 us per op, inside the ±11 % these rows resolve, but consistent in direction); `Single` arms and the Byte and Numeric shapes flat. What remains on `mixed-40k-any` is the pass count: 10 passes at 2 ns per character, of which the even-cut certificate (2 passes) and prefix reuse in the budget search (about 1) are the recorded next steps.

### Performance round 12, one walk near the floor instead of three (2026-09-17)

**Done.** The round set out to use the even cut as a certificate: the whole text's plan gives the fewest symbols any split can use, and if the text cut into that many equal character counts fits the capacity, the count is settled without the walk at the capacity, and the same ceiling settles a scan candidate of its count indicator band without the scan walk. It worked on the benchmark's shape (8.9 passes to 7.0) and nowhere else, and measuring why changed the design. Over digit-and-word mixtures, alphanumeric, Latin-1 and UTF-8 content, content whose density changes along the text and seeded random runs, the balanced budget sits 3 to 22 bits above the plan's floor on all of them, while the even cut's fullest chunk is within 55 bits of that floor only on periodic content: on the rest it is 139 to 11,686 bits over and usually past the capacity, so it certified nothing and, as the bracket's ceiling since round 6, had been leaving those searches eight to ten probes wide. The repeated lines of `mixed-40k-any` are the even cut's best case and had hidden it. `TryPlan` now takes the whole text's plan first and walks once at the floor plus 31 bits at the largest version, limited to the bound's count: the walk holding it settles the count, settles every scan candidate of the same band whose capacity is at least the walk's budget (a chunk's cost depends on the version only through the band, so that split fits as it is), and is the budget search's ceiling with its split kept as the settled one. The even cut and `BracketBalancedBudget` are gone. Where the answer's band has no such walk the search opens from the floor in widening steps (31, 31 again, then tripling), each failure raising the floor; the first walk is attempted only when the bound's count leaves each symbol two margins of slack; and a text that fits one single-mode symbol is answered by the walk's closed form before any plan is taken, which the first cut of the certificate had broken (2.5 times slower on the one-symbol path, caught by the scenario added for it). Every shortcut is a bound or a split that exists, so the plan is the one the three searches alone find. `StructuredAppendPlannerTest` gains eleven rows on its three-property test, against the walk that prices one character at a time: periodic content at version 40, digits then the mixture, prose then digits, seeded random runs, ranges that cross a band (9/10, 26/27), and pair-heavy content whose balanced budget sits 32 to 47 bits above the floor, which is what runs the widening steps. Mutations: a scan shortcut that ignores the capacity fails one case and a count accepted from a failed walk fails three; dropping the band from the scan shortcut fails nothing, and correctly, since a lower band's narrower count indicators only make the same split cheaper, so that condition is conservative rather than load-bearing; a widening step that does not raise the floor fails nothing because it only costs probes. Full suite green on both target frameworks (10,586 on net10.0, 10,573 on net8.0). `QRCodeStructuredAppendEncode` gains `uneven-40k-any`, digits followed by order lines, so the benchmark holds a shape that is not periodic.

**Lessons.** A bound is only as good as the content it was measured on, and a benchmark made of one repeated line is the best case of anything that assumes evenness: the ceiling that looked tight for six rounds was tight on that shape alone. Ask where the answer sits relative to each end of a bracket on content that differs in kind, not in length; here one table answered it (the floor is tight everywhere, the ceiling almost nowhere) and the table cost a minute. A certificate has to be asked after the cheap answers, not before them: the one-symbol case needs no plan at all, and the first cut paid for one. And a second attempt is not a smaller version of the first failure: trying the floor walk again 32 bits higher for pair-heavy content doubled the waste, because on that content the first walk fails when the bound's count is out of reach, not when the margin is short, which is what the slack condition now tests for.

**Benchmark delta.** Counted, passes of the program per plan (the per-symbol writer's pass excluded): `mixed-40k-any` 8.92 → 7.00, the same text pinned to version 40 7.99 → 7.00, `mixed-4k-max10` 8.92 → 7.83, digits then order lines 7.97 → 5.00, seeded random runs 10.90 → 7.00, a Japanese mixture 7.88 → 7.00, one symbol 0 → 0, pair-heavy content at level H 9.99 → 9.92; no shape above its baseline. Timed, `QRCodeStructuredAppendEncode`, ShortRun, a worktree at the previous commit against this tree with the same benchmark file, three rounds alternating: `mixed-40k-any` `Optimal` 2.03 / 2.09 / 2.02 → 1.80 / 1.84 / 1.83 ms (−11 %), `uneven-40k-any` `Optimal` 2.20 / 1.70 / 1.64 → 1.37 / 1.40 / 1.40 ms (−18 % on the medians); `Single` arms and the shapes whose searches run as `Single` within noise. One run-state outlier that is not the change: the untouched `Symbols` arm of `mixed-40k-any` read 1.6 and 1.8 ms in the first two rounds on this tree and 0.82 in the third, with its `Single` arm, which contains it, at 0.83 to 0.86 throughout. Tried and not kept: pricing the even cut's chunks as eight lanes of one AVX2 program, one vector per state, measured at 4.6 times the scalar pricing (a gather for the eight characters and sixteen AVX-512 lanes both lost to it), because the design that replaced the even cut has no cut to price; the same step is the natural kernel for walking several budget probes at once, which is the next round, with prefix reuse.

### Performance round 13, the budget search walked eight budgets at a time (2026-09-17)

**Done.** After round 12 a plan under `Optimal` was seven passes of the segmentation program on every content: the whole text's plan, the walk near the floor, and five bisection probes inside its 31-bit bracket. The round was asked to reuse the leading chunks of a walk that held the count, and that is in: a chunk's end is monotone in the budget, so a probe between a failed budget and a held one shares the leading chunks on which those two walks agree and resumes after them, with no chunk's cost needed (the planner now keeps the ends of the last failed walk beside the settled one, and `CountChunks` resumes). Counting what it saves is what moved the round: 0.6 of 7 passes on periodic content and nothing on the rest, because a greedy chunk is filled to within a character of its budget, so two walks more than a character apart in budget part ways at their first chunk and only the last probe or two of a bisection share anything; the 1.1 passes round 11's analysis had projected were for the even-cut bracket that round 12 removed. The probes themselves are the larger target: they are independent instances of one program over one text, so up to eight budgets now walk at once in `StructuredAppendPlanner.Lanes.cs`, one budget per lane of a 256-bit vector and one vector per state. A lane whose chunk closes re-reads the character that did not fit and falls a step behind, which keeps the lanes within a few characters of each other; while they are at one character, which is nearly always, a step is the scalar loop's class lookup and branches over vector adds and mins and costs about one scalar step for the eight, and around a chunk end they are stepped separately with the class and byte cost per lane in scalar code. A lane that has failed keeps closing chunks unrecorded, or it would run ahead and the lanes would never be together again. The first batch is the walk near the floor itself (eight budgets 3 to 31 bits above it; 5 to 47 under UTF-8, whose three-byte characters put balanced budgets up to 46 bits above the floor), settling the count, the band's versions, the ceiling and, by its failed neighbour, the floor; a second batch takes every budget left between them; where no walk has bracketed the answer's band the bracket opens by a batch as well. A plan is the whole text's plan and two batches, in every charset. A byte order mark keeps the scalar walks, and so does content whose chunks average under 128 characters, where the lanes are rarely together (78-character chunks ran half as slow again with lanes, 267-character ones nearly twice as fast). Only `Vector256`'s portable surface is used, behind `NET8_0_OR_GREATER` and `Vector256.IsHardwareAccelerated`; elsewhere the scalar probes run with the shared-chunk resume. `TryPlan` gains an internal overload that turns the lanes off, which is what lets `StructuredAppendLaneWalkTest` require the plan to be the same plan either way (eleven texts, six ranges, four levels, with and without a byte order mark) and hold the lane walk to the scalar walk lane by lane, from the start and resumed, at budgets one, four and thirteen bits apart across five versions, with pairs, lone surrogates and an interior U+FEFF. Mutations: a lane stepping back one character instead of two after closing on a pair's second half fails 3 cases, sharing one chunk too many fails 25, a byte run that ignores the budget fails 30; a failed lane that stops closing fails nothing, being a cost only; and dropping the rule that a pair is not judged on its first half failed nothing either, which turned out to be the code's fault rather than the tests': a pair is priced whole on its first half, so a budget it breaks is broken on both halves and the chunk ends before the pair either way, and the rule was removed from the lanes. Full suite green on both target frameworks (10,608 on net10.0, 10,595 on net8.0). `QRCodeStructuredAppendEncode` gains `utf8-15k-mixed`, Japanese sentences carrying order numbers, since the existing UTF-8 shape holds no run a plan helps and its searches never run the program.

**Lessons.** Count before building: the requested reuse was exact and cheap to write, and one table of passes showed it was worth a twelfth of what the analysis two rounds earlier had promised, because that analysis was made against a bracket the round in between had replaced; an estimate carries the design it was made under.
